newsitem.title: USA: GM faces new strike threat from supplier plant.
newsitem.headline: GM faces new strike threat from supplier plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp. headed into the weekend Friday still trying to settle an eight-day Indiana truck plant strike and facing the threat of a walkout at a key supplier of starter motors.
A total of 1,600 United Auto Workers union members in Indiana and Mississippi were poised to strike at midnight Friday at Delco Remy America Inc.

Negotiators for the Anderson, Ind.-based company, made up of former GM operations, are trying to reach a new three-year contract. It was the first set of negotiations since the company was purchased by a management group lead by former Chrysler Corp. executive Harold Sperlich in 1994.

UAW members want the components maker to follow the pattern agreement set by Detroit's Big Three and other suppliers, as well as hire permanently about 440 temporary workers in Anderson, union officials said.
"All I know is they are continuing to meet, and the strike deadline is midnight tonight," said John Coale, vice president of UAW Local 662 in Anderson.
Strike signs have already been drawn up, as well as schedules for walking picket lines in case union leaders call for a walkout, Coale said.
A representative from Delco Remy could not be reached for comment Friday. The company makes starter motors for nearly all of GM's North American-built cars and light trucks.

Delco Remy is the second supplier spun off from GM to go down to the wire on contract negotiations. Last month, American Axle & Manufacturing Inc. reached new contract terms minutes before a strike deadline set by the UAW.
In those talks, American Axle agreed to follow the Big Three pattern, which calls for lump-sum payments of $2,000 in the first year and 3 percent raises in the second and third years.
The contracts also include a guarantee to maintain employment at 95 percent of the current work force level over the life of the agreement and generous improvments in pension benefits.

Because of the just-in-time inventory system automakers use, GM could run out of starter motors within two days of a strike. Privately, GM officials were not expressing too much concern over the talks. GM spokesman Tom Klipstine said the company is watching the situation, but declined to comment further.

Meantime, negotiations continued at GM's Fort Wayne, Ind., full-size pickup truck plant, where 2,700 United Auto Workers union members walked off the job March 14 after the two sides failed to agree on terms for a new local contract.

Tom Beaman, a spokesman for GM's Truck Group, said bargaining was scheduled to continue until 5 p.m. EST Friday, then resume at 10 a.m. Saturday. The plant, one of four GM full-size pickup truck plants in North America, makes regular-cab versions of the Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra.
"We still have trucks in the pipeline, we still have trucks getting to dealers. Right now we just want to focus on the talks," he said.
Union leaders at Local 2209, who want GM to hire more workers to reduce overtime, could not be reached for comment Friday. Earlier this week, they said progress was slow.
